text: Denis Phillips I have followed you since I moved to Florida May 30,2004 from Indiana. It was a summer to remember. But you were the only meteorologist that was giving facts and calm details. I did get an alarm call and had to drive to my work during Charlie. That was scary but I remained calm got what was needed done. I had started calling you suspender man that first night too funny. Please do not ever retire we need you. You are by far the most professional and knowledgeable meteorologist around. The only time I get scared is when Jim Cantore comes to town. text: Just prepare. Prepare for flooding. Figure out your evacuation route. Generators, batteries, water and food, cook food on propane first that may spoil, know your flood zone (it will be a new moon, so tide may be higher), get anything valuable off of the ground in advance if you are in a flood zone or surge zone. If you only have one safe way out, consider going further inland for a night or two to prevent being stuck. If you stay, have a life vest or something floaty. Get one for the puppers. Emergency use cases, it comes in handy and can lessen some stress. Seal important documents, and have some cash. Have gas, don't be a gas hog at the station. Don't stress. Use common sense. This happens every year, take it serious, but don't freak out over it. Just have a plan, practice the plan, and execute. And if it doesn't happen... yay! Party.

text:
Same as most of them: We know the potential is brewing out there, it's just Way Too early to get a more defined path. Best thing to do is stop panicking, make sure you're stocked up on necessary supplies (water, non-perishables, toiletries, batteries, a weather radio if you have one, Pet food, etc.) & make sure you have a full gas tank. Then just sit back and wait and see.
These storms can be so unpredictable, and even at the last minute when you're almost Certain it's going to make landfall at a particular point, it can shift drastically and come in at a totally different spot. Just don't get caught unprepared. 🤷‍♀️
Noone knows for sure what is going to be, or where is going to head yet. Noone can make decisions on your vacation plans/travel but You. It's like a broken record EVERY storm with these questions.

author: Denis Phillips
text: have an evacuation plan in case you are evacuated. Have cash on hand as there will be no way to use credit/debit cards if the power goes out. Keep your car full of gas. The lines will be crazy. Have 2 weeks of meds available. Have plenty of pet food, at least 2 weeks. Have flashlights and batteries on hand. If you think you will need a generator get it now. There will be none the day after a hurricane hits. Make a list of things to take if you have to evacuate. Don’t wait until the last minute when a hurricane is 2 hours away. You won’t be able to get anywhere because there will be a lot of traffic backed up. Don’t let people minimize the seriousness of a hurricane by saying things like “they always say it’s going to be bad”, “we evacuated once but nothing happened so we won’t leave again”, or “it’s going to be nothing”. Those things may be true but it’s better to be safe than sorry. Hope this helps.

text: Ohio here… at what level storm do you typically have to evacuate?

author: Denis Phillips
text: depends on where you are in FL. Run from water. Hide from the wind. I’m not in a flood zone and 20 miles inland or so. I’m in a house built after 2015. I likely would never evacuate. It would never be ordered here anyway.

author: Denis Phillips
text: Usually you’re ordered to evacuate based on your flood zone. There is a map that tells you. Your county puts out a notice saying which zones need to evacuate for floods. Any level storm can bring floods. For wind, typically for a category 1 or above, mobile/manufactured homes are ordered to evacuate. Between category 1 and 3, there is a lot of discretion for those who live in regular housing. Some people evacuate for everything, some prefer to shelter in place but will evacuate for a cat 3 or higher, it kind of depends on your situation and the individual storm. You have a few days to watch what it’s doing. There is a bit of a gamble as the storm’s trajectory can change; I remember one storm (I think Charlie) where a lot of people evacuated into its path. Gas is a commodity, as is space on the road, so everybody can’t evacuate every time. I’ve never experienced being in the path of a category 4 or 5, but I think mandatory evacuations may apply for those almost always.

text:
Here's a suggestion to ensure your furry friend's safety during severe tropical storms. Consider purchasing a small pool or inflatable item for under $10 from Walmart or a similar store. Place it in your garage or a secure area of your home. If your garage is noisy and you have a small dog, opt for a toddler pool. You can still use sod or pee pads, but remember to work with your pet and reassure them. Playing soft music during the storm and consulting with your veterinarian can also be helpful. There are various options available, such as special vests, blankets, and medications.
By placing some sod, grass, and perhaps a bit of their waste, you can create a designated area for them to relieve themselves. This will help them sense that it's their space. Place a snack nearby and walk with them to the pool, supporting them as needed. Praise your dog when they use it as their bathroom. This simple measure can provide peace of mind and ensure everyone's safety during inclement weather. Feel free to share this tip with other pet owners, and if you have a different suggestion, please share it as well. We're all in this together. Good luck!

text: The thing is that even though I’m sure Denis would be happy to help , there just isn’t any way of knowing by anyone. .I’ve been here all my life as my family before me ( I’m 85) and we’re dealing with nature.Ive seen these things stall, turn , stall again , do a u turn , you name it. Even the National Hurricane e Center ( where all the info comes from) will not say exactly until a system is closer and better developed . Even then, they will say “ expected” to do this or that. Folks are expecting way too much too soon. Years ago we didn’t know a storm was even out there till it was almost on top of us. Just stay tuned to Denis , local stations, etc and as it gets closer , or larger ( if it does) you’ll be able to judge. Facts 🛑
Q: What are Potential Tropical Cyclone Advisories?
A: These are issued before a tropical depression or tropical storm forms.
Q: What purpose do these advisories serve?
A: They provide the NWS with the ability to issue a watch with a full 48 hours of lead time or a warning with a full 36 hours of lead time prior to possible tropical storm, hurricane, or life-threatening storm surge conditions on land.
Q: What information should we expect?
ALL of us should see information containing all of the standard NHC advisory text and graphical products and should be issued at the standard advisory times, according to the Federal Government, NOAA/NWS.

text:
One thing to remember is that regardless of the actual weather, first responders are often mandated to work well before a storm hits to assist with medical evacuations, like ventilator dependent patients who do not have a reliable generator. They are also often mandated well after a storm to support not only the normal 911 volume but the post-storm freak out callers and ones who were criminally unprepared.
So please, if you see a first responder in line at the store tomorrow, be kind as they are probably preparing for a rough few days away from their families.

Soft Pumpkin Snickerdoodles 🎃
Delicious and easy Pumpkin Snickerdoodles infused with pumpkin puree and warming spices!
Ingredients:
1/2 cup butter, softened
1 1/2 cups sugar
1 egg
1/2 cup pumpkin puree
3 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon cream of tartar
2 teaspoons baking soda
1/4 teaspoon salt
1 teaspoon pumpkin pie spice or 1/2 teaspoon cinnamon, 1/4 teaspoon allspice, 1/4 teaspoon nutmeg, 1/4 teaspoon ginger
Cinnamon Sugar Mixture:
2 tablespoons sugar
2 teaspoons cinnamon
Instructions:
Preheat your oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit (175 degrees Celsius). Line a baking sheet with parchment paper. In a large mixing bowl, cream together the softened butter, sugar, egg, and pumpkin puree until smooth. Add the flour, cream of tartar, baking soda, salt, and pumpkin pie spice (or individual spices). Mix until a dough forms. In a small bowl, mix together the sugar and cinnamon for the cinnamon sugar coating. Roll the dough i-inch balls, then roll each ball in the cinnamon sugar mixture until coated evenly. Place the coated dough balls on the prepared baking sheet, spacing them evenly. Lightly press down on each dough ball with the back of a spoon or your fingers to slightly flatten. Bake in the preheated oven for 8-10 minutes, or until the edges are set and the cookies are just beginning to crack on top. Remove from the oven and let the cookies cool on the baking sheet for a few minutes before transferring them to a wire rack to cool completely. Enjoy these soft and flavorful Pumpkin Snickerdoodles!
My Notes: the dough is very sticky, I recommend refrigerating it for 15-20 minutes before scooping and in-between scooping each sheet. I used a 1 1/4" scoop and did not press the cookies down.
Using a 12"x18" sheet, I was able to get 15 cookies per sheet and made a total of 51 cookies. They are tasty, but I think I might add 1/2 tsp more of the Pumpkin pie spice next time.

author: Denis Phillips
text: Helpful ideas if anyone needs during times like this with tropical storms and hurricanes. If you have an Ice maker or you buy a bag of ice separate your ice into frozen Ziploc bags and place those in your fridge at the coldest temperature. Place frozen and quart size baggies in your drawers where you keep your cheeses or any type of produce to keep cold extra cold in case of power outage. I do this every year and it really helps if the power goes out your food will stay cold and you can use an ice chest too as well. Right now I have 3 frozen gallon size bag Ziploc in the middle section of my fridge since last night and the ice cubes are still frozen. Today I did the quart size for the drawers.so do as many as you need and zip them tight. I hope this helps anyone that needs it

text:
Many yrs ago I was living in a different county in Florida. I got a green light to cross US 41. So glad, I was smart enough to pause before moving forward. A flatbed tow truck ran the red light and passed the intersection, came to a stop, awkwardly, at the median side of the road.(Assuming, health emergency). Fast forward a week later..
Worked all day, didn't feel like cooking. Drove to the 7-11 to get a sandwich. Wind was wicked crazy when I got there. Retail stores behind there had left shopping carts out. Blowing around like crazy. Double doors of 7-11 where propped open because they were getting a delivery. I took one step inside and my hair decided it was in a race to get inside first! Lol. Picked out a sandwich and went to check out, power went out. As I was driving home (without said sandwich), I realized I was driving over something. Waited the storm out, went to another convenience store hours later. Overheard an employee talking to an EMT. There had been a tornado. It hit a business selling storage sheds. I had been driving over the remnants of them!! My coworkers teased me for a while. Asking me if I had a death wish and calling me Dorothy! 😂 Reasons why I stay inside and prepare before hand.

text: A couple tips you may not have thought of (Hurricane Michael survivor): Get a box of cheap solar driveway lights (they come in the cardboard case with holes they sit in). Put them outside during the day and they will light up a large area inside most of the night and you (and your kids) can walk around with one like a lantern without any batteries or FIRE. If you want hot water, you can paint a couple buckets black, cover them with foil and set them in the driveway during the day. A lot of water gets wasted leaving those bottles laying around and forgetting them.

text: ucf is much further south then uf. It's currently heading toward fsu (might as well keep using the schools as location markers ). Historically storms that come in from this angle, this time of year and with the low pressure system out there fighting with Helene it has set up a situation anyone who has lived here for years can spot from a mile away. They always bop and weave, zig and zag but they tend to do a last minute hook to the east, or northeast and if that happened it sets the situation toward uf and away from fsu. In order to target ucf it would have to happen sooner OR it would have to bank much harder and much faster which should have signs that are louder and already hinting at. (This is not the case. I try to set up the pre storm chaos by deciding what can I live with after if the storm does hit or doesn't. I err on the side of - I would rather be a little annoyed and worn out from doing more things then I ended up needing to do VERSUS the other way around. At a certain point though people can scare themselves into doing something that ends up putting them in a different kind of danger. I acknowledge that florida has a lot of people and evacuations during a chaotic time creates dangerous situations on roadways and such. UCF is more in the zone as of now anyways- people who do need to evacuate are heading that way. Orlando seems like a solid safe destination for anyone on the west coast in Tampa Bay. text: Approximately what time will we know #2 from Denis' post above? (2. It ALL boils down to where this low is once it enters the Gulf. The steering currents are pretty much locked down. We said this yesterday. If the center is over the tip of the Yucatan tomorrow, the track should go more Panhandle/Big Bend. author: Denis Phillips
text: Sez Meta AI: "Tropical cyclones, cyclones, and hurricanes are all types of storm systems that form over warm ocean waters. The primary difference between them is the geographical area in which they occur. Tropical Cyclone: This is a general term used by meteorologists to describe a rotating, organized system of clouds and thunderstorms that forms over warm tropical waters. Tropical cyclones can form in any tropical ocean and are also known as tropical storms or typhoons. Cyclone: This term is specifically used in the Indian Ocean and the southern Pacific Ocean. Cyclones are tropical cyclones that form in these regions and are typically characterized by strong winds and heavy rainfall. Hurricane: This term is used in the Atlantic Ocean, the Caribbean Sea, and the Gulf of Mexico. Hurricanes are tropical cyclones that form in these regions and are known for their strong winds, heavy rainfall, and storm surges." Thus endeth the lesson LOL

author: Denis Phillips
text: This is what my husband's aunt who's lived here for 30 plus years said. Which is worse: the right or left side of a hurricane? Tropical cyclones are typically pretty symmetrical, meaning heavy winds and rains are dispersed pretty evenly throughout the system. But hurricanes move more and have a less symmetrical make-up, meaning there’s a side of the storm that’s more intense and dangerous than the other, with stronger winds. This is often called the “dirty side” of a hurricane and is on the right side, in Helene's case the east side, of a hurricane.

author: Denis Phillips
text: On or near water” refers to areas directly along the coastline, bays, rivers, or other bodies of water, as well as low-lying areas that are within several miles of the shore and at risk of storm surge. This includes properties that are not directly waterfront but are in flood-prone evacuation zones like Zone A or have low elevations, typically below 10 feet above sea level. The risk area can extend 1 to 10 miles inland, depending on the geography and the strength of the storm. If you’re in one of these areas, you could experience water pushed ashore by the storm, even if you’re not right next to the coast.

author: Denis Phillips
text: Storm A can pass by further out then storm B and cause higher tides and anything else they want because storms are not made equal. They are different sizes, moving at different speeds, they can have more/less moisture from each other...and on and on. As a storm approaches the water is typically sucked out and away from shore line and then as it moves past the area the water is basically pushed back in. There are plenty of videos online that show visuals of the science of it all. This is why the water was sucked out of tampa Bay during the last storm (?) (Or maybe the one before- we seem to have them yearly and I can't remember which one did what at this point). Sometimes it's best to remember we are talking about Mother Nature here and hurricanes. They are not a one size fits all and can behave differently from one storm to the next. Staybsafe

author: Denis Phillips
text: what’s an eye wall replacement?

author: Denis Phillips
text: I just googled it because I had no idea either. Apparently it happens when a new eyewall develops around the original smaller and more compact eyewall. Once a hurricane reaches its peak intensity, the outer bands strengthen and organize into a ring of thunderstorms, making a new outer eyewall. The outer eyewall overtakes the initial eyewall, causing it to collapse.

author: Denis Phillips
text: I think the rule is when it is a CAT 4 - just go. I rode out Irma and I will admit, it was terrifying. And Irma was flirting with Cat 5 at one point but when it went through the Everglades, it lost power and dropped to CAT 3 at the last minute. I think the official records have it as a 4 now. But if Irma had a storm surge component to it (we are far inland) - then I would have just left. The storm surge numbers they are talking about are crazy and life-threatening. Ian was a prime example - we weren’t even in the cone and the storm surge flooded a large section of the city. People were live-streaming to the local news about needing to be rescued from their houses because the first floor landing completely flooded. So no matter what size storm, sure…be concerned about the wind…but also pay attention to the storm surge. The wind is dangerous but the surge is sneaky and can come hours afterwards and out you in danger. That is what we are experiencing right now. Parts of Naples is flooding right now due to the storm surge from Helene.

author: Denis Phillips
text: if you still have water in your house then yes keep power off. If it’s all receded and electrical items seem dry power can probably be turned back on. I would unplug any expensive item like computer, tvs, appliances before turning it back on just in case it surges or is still wet. Opening windows and any air movement will help drying and preventing mold. Fans are a big help. Dehumidifiers as well. But ultimately you’ll will need a flood cut and proper fans if the water truly flooded. That is where dry me out comes in. Dragging wet stuff out will be up to the discretion of the homeowner. If it’s something they want to salvage then either put it in the sun or let it dry out if it’s something small. If it’s gonna be trashed then definitely pull it out. Something a lot of people don’t think of during a flood is your ac. They aren’t meant to be direct contact with saltwater. That system will need checked and cleaned if not outright replaced if it was submerged. Recommend either Jonny cool or progressive air for that.

author: Denis Phillips
text: Prayer for the Victims of Storms and Disasters Almighty and Merciful Father, We come before You today with hearts full of compassion for all the victims of storms, hurricanes, floods, and other natural disasters that have impacted lives and communities. We pray for Your protection and comfort over those who have lost their homes, their loved ones, and at times even their hope. Lord, send Your peace to those who are in confusion and distress. We ask for healing for the wounded, restoration for broken families, and provision for those who have lost everything. Lord, be a refuge for those walking through these storms. We pray that Your light and presence would shine in the midst of darkness. Comfort those who are grieving and give them the strength to carry on. We know You are a God of mercy and justice, and we ask that You bring healing and restoration to all who have been affected. Let Your will be done, and may Your glory be revealed even in the midst of these trials. In the mighty name of Jesus Christ, we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, as we lift up prayers for the victims of these natural disasters, let us not forget that these storms are a reminder to us all. Just as we rush to repair damaged roofs before the rain returns, so too must we tend to our spiritual lives. The Bible warns us that difficult days are coming and today is the day to repair the broken places in our hearts. Jesus Himself warned us in Scripture that perilous times would come, and He calls us to be ready. The Lord said in Matthew 24:42: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know on what day your Lord will come.” Let us not be distracted by the temporary things of this world. Just as those on the roof during a storm cannot afford to come down, we cannot afford to be distracted from the salvation of our souls when the storms of life rage. Today is the day of salvation! There is no time to waste. The disasters and sufferings we witness in the world around us are a reminder that this earth is not our permanent home. God is calling us to be prepared for eternity, to turn away from our sins, and to embrace His gift of salvation. A Call to Salvation: Prepare Before It’s Too Late Dear friends, salvation is a gift that God offers to every one of us. We do not know what tomorrow will bring, but today, we have the opportunity to receive Jesus Christ into our lives. He is the one who mends what is broken, heals our wounds, and grants us eternal life. If you have not yet given your life to Jesus, now is the time to do so. Don’t wait for the next storm to come before seeking refuge in Him. The Lord is calling you today to come to Him, to allow His love to embrace and save you. Jesus bore your sins, your burdens, and your pains on the cross so that you could be free. Prayer of Salvation Lord Jesus, I come to You today with a humble heart. I acknowledge that I am a sinner and that I need Your forgiveness. I believe You died on the cross for my sins and rose again to give me eternal life. I ask You to come into my life, cleanse me, and restore me. I want to follow You all the days of my life and walk in Your light. Thank You for Your love and salvation. Amen. If you prayed this prayer, know that you have just taken the most important step of your life. Don’t let the storms of this world take your eyes off the peace and salvation that Jesus offers. May God guide you and protect you every day, and may His light shine on you, now and forever. God bless you!

author: Denis Phillips
text:
if you’re asking which is “wrong” and which is “right” then you’re completely misunderstanding the point of models. They are all projections based on probabilities and at this point, none of them are likely to hit.
For example, ESPN now has computer models that say the KC chiefs are a 98% probability to make the playoffs.Now I’m not sure what goes into their model, but I’m sure some of their model is accounting for the fact they are 4-0, defending champs, and have a solid roster. But if Pat Mahomes slips in the shower, breaks his leg and they miss the playoffs, it won’t be because the model is “wrong”. It will be because the model couldn’t reasonably account for such an injury.
All these are is a snapshot prediction based on probability at a given time. Most will not pan out. When they don’t, the question isn’t “why is this model bad,” but rather “what variable, which this model didn’t fully account for, needs to be worked into future models?” …or in the Mahomes example “ what data can these models never accurately predict”. Sometimes the wind 5 days out falls into the latter category

text:
With all of the rain that's forecast to fall BEFORE future "Milton" arrives (wherever he ends up going)...the prospect of category 1 or even tropical storm force winds could spell major trouble for Florida's many oak trees.
Saturated ground + high winds seems like it would = a recipe for mass uprootings.
As Denis frequently says, the worst case scenario usually doesn't come to pass. I'm guessing the corollary to that is that the best case scenario usually doesn't come to pass either. So...it's somewhere in the middle.
Based on these recent model trends, I'm starting to get a little concerned that the "middle" scenario in this case may still result in a lot of trees coming down on roofs, cars, etc.
Hoping for that best case scenario to materialize!

The roof's design includes a slant that goes from 225 feet above second base to 85 feet above the center field wall. author: Denis Phillips
text:
Prayers from South Carolina to those in the path in Hurricane Milton. May you shelter in the hand of God Almighty. God is bigger than this storm, bigger than the wind and water. To my praying brothers and sisters, I encourage you to join me in to ask Him to shield those in danger, and to calm the wind and waves.
During Helene, I was in NC and legit scared. My team sent me verses that gave me strength and a lot of comfort - Matthew 8 and Psalm 91. Also highly recommend Psalm 23. I read them out loud, over and over. I sang worship songs to help drown out the storm. It helped me get through things, praying that perhaps someone out there will take comfort in these words too.
Remember, even in the darkest moments, God is with you and He loves you.

author: Denis Phillips
text: I spent a good amount of time tracking this storm continually watching news reports and checking various weather sites for wind probabilities in my area (Riverview, FL). I just kept hearing that the worst winds would cover a narrow band of maybe 10-15 miles from the eye. It was never mention anywhere that the eye wall would expand to such a size that a 100+ mph swath of wind would ultimately march across all of Hillsborough county, plus several surrounding counties. Currently, at 7:54 EDT, the National Weather Service is showing we will experienced wind gusts of 108 mph at 12 Midnight, despite the Extreme Wind Warning only running through 9:30pm. Perhaps the warning will eventually be extended? Very surprised by this development, to say the least. This must be a very uncommon phenomena.

Stay safe and good luck to all in Milton's path!

text:
Say this out loud, all who is reading this.
Heavenly Father,
We come before You today, standing in the gap for Florida, a state beloved by many. We acknowledge Your sovereignty over the heavens and the earth, over the winds and the waters. You, who once commanded the storm to be still, we invoke Your divine authority now.
Lord, protect Florida and its inhabitants. Shield them under Your mighty wings. Let Your peace that surpasses all understanding guard their hearts and minds in Christ Jesus. Provide comfort for the anxious, strength for the weary, and hope for the despairing.
Lord Jesus, who walked on water and calmed the sea, we ask that You command the hurricane approaching Florida to dissipate. In the name of Jesus Christ, we say to this storm: Be still! Let the winds die down, the rains cease, and the threat of destruction be no more. Let Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven, turning this potential for chaos into a display of Your mercy and power.
Father, should any harm come, we pray for swift recovery. Send Your Spirit to inspire acts of kindness, unity, and rapid restoration. Let communities come together, not just in survival, but in revival, showing the world what it means to be Your hands and feet.
In the name of Jesus Christ, we declare this storm's path altered, its strength diminished, and its harm minimized. We trust in Your Word, which says mountains can be moved with faith the size of a mustard seed.
We thank You, Lord, for Your unending love and for answering us when we call upon Your name. Let this prayer not only be a plea for safety but a testament to Your glory, showing that through Christ, even nature bows.
In Jesus' name, we pray.
Amen Please Thank Kathy Schulz for this prayer

text:
Heavenly Father,
As Hurricane Milton approaches, we turn to you with heavy hearts and a sense of urgency. We ask for your divine protection over all of us in its path. Surround us with your comforting presence and grant us the strength to face the challenges ahead.
Please watch over families, friends, and communities as they prepare and seek safety. Instill in us a spirit of resilience and hope, even as the storm looms. We pray for first responders and emergency workers, that they may be kept safe as they serve and protect those in need.
Lord, may your peace be felt in the hearts of those who are anxious and fearful. Help them find comfort in one another and in the knowledge that they are not alone. As the winds and rains come, we ask for your guidance and support for all those affected, that we may be able to rebuild and recover.
We trust in your mercy and grace, and we seek your protection over every life touched by this storm. Amen.

Jesus hear our prayers
Heavenly Father,
We come before You with humble hearts, seeking Your protection over the Gulf states, especially Florida, as Hurricane Milton approaches. Lord, You are the Creator of all things, and even the winds and the waves obey You. We ask that You calm this storm and shield the people in its path.
In Your mercy, place Your mighty hand over the land and sea. We pray for the safety of every family, home, and community. Guard them under the shelter of Your wings, and let no harm come near. Strengthen those who are preparing and give wisdom to all who are working to keep others safe.
We stand on the promises of Psalm 91: “He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will rest in the shadow of the Almighty.” May Your presence be the refuge for all who face this storm. Let Your peace, which surpasses all understanding, reign in their hearts, and let Your protection be their shield and defense.
In the powerful name of Jesus, we pray. Amen.

text:
FYI, if you have an iPhone 14 or later, I would highly recommend upgrading to the latest iOS 18.x before the worst of the storm gets here to be able to make use of satellite messaging that works without cellular service nor Wi-Fi in emergencies, just in case that happens and it’s necessary. See apple link at bottom for how and to try the demo test to make sure you know it works.
The feature only got released September 16, 2024 when iOS 18 came out and it includes an ability to send iMessage or SMS text message via satellite if Wi-Fi or cellular is down, and not just to emergency services. It does require a view of the sky to work, so debatably would be more useful after pouring rain stops.
I would also recommend turning on Find My Friends and adding a couple extended family members just in case so they can at least know where you are or where you were last your phone battery dies. These are just things I’m doing, feel free not to, just wanted to advise in case others don’t know about it as I haven’t heard it mention much in any weather reporters prep list.
The satellite messaging is a three week old feature, so not many people know about it. It greatly helped a friend of mine in North Carolina near Asheville stay in touch with love ones when the cell towers and service failed.

Father, as disaster swirls around me, keep me in the shadow of Your wing. Direct and unite my heart to fear and to honor only You. Your promise was not to keep me from storms or strife but to be with me.
Thank You, my Master, for Your presence and power. Thank You for the gift of Your Son who lives inside me, strengthening and empowering me for the large and the little, the majestic and the mundane.
Lord, I pray for my friends who are hurting today. The winds tear at their lives; the pummeling doesn’t seem to stop. Help these dear ones reach the center in You. In quietness and trust is their strength, O God. May they find a place of sure refuge. May they see these storms and these circumstances as Your instruments of trust.
Today, Lord Jesus, help us choose You. Help us to seek first Your kingdom and Your righteousness. Help us look beyond the storm to see Your peace that passes understanding. And help us hold fast to what is good—only You. In Your holy name I pray—AMEN.

text:
here you go professor...A wobble in a hurricane is a small movement in the storm's path, either to the left or right. Meteorologists use the term to describe how a major hurricane deviates from its projected path.
Wobbles can be important because they determine the hurricane's destination and the amount of damage it will cause. For example, a slight wobble in a hurricane's path can significantly impact where storm surge occurs.
To track wobbles, meteorologists use a combination of data from satellites, radar, the storm's forecast trajectory, and its previous path. This information is used to show how the storm's path is changing in real time.

text: The speed/category of Milton is so concerning to forecasters because the more powerful the storm over sea, the larger the surge. It will flood to levels never seen before and have power behind it, leading to inundations over historic markers. If you can get to a higher elevation, please do. The 12 ft elevation of your house, vs a 10-15 inundation ? Your house will not win, you will be left stranded. The water level alone will flood the house, but the power (basically the speed of the water) will be high. The water does not rise slowly and still, it will push at pillars, foundations, all structural elements. Even to find somewhere 5-10 miles inland, at 20 elevation or higher, would be better.

A couple more I have done per an emergency responder friend:
1) Remove all outside hoses from the house. These can become projectiles in high wind & if enough force could damage the pipe
2) Latch the garage door from the inside (latches are on the door) Most don’t even know the latches are there. This may keep the door from flying up in extreme winds
3) If you have pets, prepare a place in the garage for them to use (kiddy pool with pee pads or a piece of artificial turf)
4) If you have an iPhone install the latest update. This will allow satellite use in case cell service is down
Stay safe everyone! These updates are so appreciated

Great list! A couple of our tips to add:
- The fuller a freezer is, the longer to thaw. Fill open spaces with containers of water to freeze (bottled water is good for this but kids may be tempted to pull the frozen water out when the power is out, door needs to stay closed.)
- Garbage cans of water for flushing: Absolutely essential but is a serious drowning hazard for children, so secure the lid if you can (temporarily duct-tape shut, etc).
- Don’t ignore boil-water notices. You don’t want to be heaving up your hurricane supplies for days in the hot sun so that you won’t use up your flushing water.

text: Keep in mind just because your electronics are “powered off” the power source is still active and on “standby”. A power fluctuation, as in a drop in voltage or a spike will fry the power source. Also turn OFF your water heater. A “brown out” drop in voltage” can burn up the heater. As voltage decreases, amperage increases, burning up equipment just a surely as an over voltage.

author: Denis Phillips
text:
It's at night when the upper and middle part of the atmosphere cools (because the sun is not there to heat it up) and that releases energy in the storms, which turns into winds and moisture.
With the increased winds and moisture, storms become stronger, likely pushing them further along their paths toward land.
And there's no proven scientific correlation really and one of the worse Katrina blew in several years ago at 6:10 a.m.

Cajun Navy is getting set up today in Ocala to help. United Cajun Navy is getting set up today at Paddock Mall in Ocala and they are requesting local citizen assistance for search and rescue especially those who have airboats, flat boats see link below. My apologies if this isn't allowed but trying to get the word out under the hurricane Milton circumstances.❤️🌀🇺🇲
ATTN:
RESCUE BOATS CALL TO ACTION
We need rescue capable boats. Stage by Wednesday afternoon in Ocala at the Paddock Mall.
Boats should be shallow water capable such as airboats, mud boats, jon boats or other Skiffs that are able to carry and operator, a second crew member, and a minimum of three rescuees comfortably and safely.
Life jackets for however many people your boat can carry
some type of marine VHF radio handheld or fixed, and be reliable.
There is some gas and Diesel available in Ocala, but plan on bringing enough cans of fuel for your boat especially if you run non-ethanol or high test for an airboat.
Gas stations will start getting resupplied within a couple of days.
We have some ability to cook and we have a couple of coffee makers.
You need to be able to get some semblance of rest so be comfortable sleeping in your truck or possibly bring air mattresses and a tent or be able to sleep in a travel trailer.
Our need is going to be greater than expected and we have also had a few people who have said they were coming that have stopped responding and is understandable since most of the people from this area are having to deal with this hurricane and their personal lives as well.
Text Larry Walker with your vessel type, name, and any other assets you can bring at: 850-582-2707
Please text only and be sure to include your name.

text:
Just a bit of comic relief...amongst all this uncertainty and scare. Thought you might enjoy this from my daughter -If you know me well, you know I have a weird thing about changing lyrics to fit life. Here is today's version....
Twas the night before Milton and all through the town
All the creatures were stirring, and running around
The shutters were hung on the windows with care,
Though hope was that Milton would not soon would be there;
The children were nestled all snug in their beds,
While visions of school closings danced in their heads;
I’m logging on Facebook, staying up late
Waiting for the latest Denis Phillips update.
When, what to my wondering eyes should appear,
But the whipping of wind, barely slowed by the sheer.
With storm surge and pressure, and lighting built-in,
I knew in a moment it must be Milton.
More rapid than eagles this hurricane came,
It wibbled, and wobbled, calling counties by name;
“Hernado or Pasco? Sarasota, Manatee?
Pinellas or Charlotte or maybe Lee?
To the top of the porch! to the top of the wall!
I’ll dash away! dash away! dash away all!”
He had high speed winds and a little eyewall.
That blasted on shore, like the start of a brawl.
He was scary and loud, coming in off the shelf,
But I laughed when I saw him, in spite of myself;
We’ve been working together and planning ahead
Being hurricane prepped, we had nothing to dread;
As he flew across Florida, his winds they did whistle,
Evacuated and sheltered, we avoided his missile.
But I heard him exclaim, going back to the heaven,
“You didn’t panic at all but remembered Rule#7!”

author: Denis Phillips
text:
It's at night when the upper and middle part of the atmosphere cools (because the sun is not there to heat it up) and that releases energy in the storms, which turns into winds and moisture.
With the increased winds and moisture, storms become stronger, likely pushing them further along their paths toward land.

text:
The Network Meterologists don't give out much info on the rural, inland counties. But, they'll know where we are after the storm if we end up with widespread destruction to film for the nightly news. The old if it bleeds it leads. Sign up for local info alerts. Here's part of the latest post from Highlands County EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT, although they put out another short request for businesses to be closed by 1:30 p.m. tomorrowto make sure customers & employees are home before 2:00 p.m. when they project hurricaneforce winds to arrive in the Avon Park area.:
This is today’s final long post, so please keep reading and check back tomorrow morning for updates! IMPORTANT INFORMATION BEING SHARED!
As of 7 p.m., Hurricane Milton is a strong Category 5 storm at 165 mph, moving ENE at 9 mph, with pressure at 905 mb. The storm is 482 miles southwest of Highlands County. Hurricane Force winds extend out 30 miles and Tropical Storm Force winds extend out 140 miles. The storm is getting larger and is still expected to remain a Major Hurricane at landfall Wednesday afternoon/evening.Hurricane conditions are expected to begin Wednesday morning at the earliest, but the timing puts impacts to our area starting between 2-10 p.m. Highlands County will see sustained hurricane-force winds between 74-110 mph. The northern part of the county will see higher winds, with the Avon Park area expected to see winds at 110 mph or higher.
Your hurricane preparations should be complete now.
IMPORTANT SAFETY MESSAGE
During the storm, STAY INSIDE. DO NOT open your doors. Even if it looks calm, DO NOT GO outside. Wait until you hear or see an official message that the hurricane is over. Sometimes, the weather may calm down during the storm but then WILL QUICKLY get bad again.
Stay away from windows. You could get hurt by pieces of broken glass or flying debris during a storm. Stay in a room with no windows or go inside a closet.
🏠 After the storm passes, please stay home for the first 48 hours. We need to keep the roads clear so that first responders can respond to medical calls and get out and assess any damages. PLEASE STAY HOME! We need to let the rescuers get to the people who need help as soon as possible.VOLUNTARY EVACUATION ORDER Starting at 8 A.M. WEDNESDAY, a voluntary evacuation order will go into effect for all residents of mobile home parks, RV parks and anyone living in low-lying areas.
Please seek refuge at any of the posted shelters in Highlands County or with family and/or loved ones who live in a sturdy structure in our community. Please check back frequently for any updates or changes.
All shelters will open at 8 a.m., Wednesday.
WATCHES & WARNINGS
Highlands County is under a hurricane warning. A Hurricane Warning means hurricane-force winds are possible within the next 36 hours. This is a dangerous storm. Your hurricane preparations should be complete now.
A Flood Watch is in effect through Thursday morning for Highlands County. Heavy rainfall is expected, and Milton’s rains could lead to flooding. 5 day rainfall totals could exceed 12 inches in spots.
You should monitor later forecasts and be alert for possible flood warnings. Those living in areas prone to flooding should be prepared to take action.
What you should do now:
📺 Turn on your TV or radio to get the latest weather updates
📲 Sign up for your community's emergency alerts - http://bit.ly/hcbccalert
Please follow our social media accounts for all official and vetted information regarding Hurricane Milton response and County operations.

text:
Thanks Lisa! The men and women on the crews continue to fly the missions out of Mobile. Please keep them in your thoughts as they still have to do their jobs while their own families are directly in the path. They are all truly inspiring and a textbook definition of public service. Trust me I have been there many times and it's a very difficult thing to do. I was working ground crew but had to stay back because my oldest fractured his leg playing hockey last Thursday and wanted to be there for him at home.
And NO they are NOT "seeding" or "steering" the storms by any stretch of some misinformed politicians warped imagination. These rumours are irresponsible, dangerous and disrespectul to the men and women who literally put their lives on the line to provide information to help protect others.
Be safe and take care!

I don’t know who wrote this but it pretty much sums up what most Floridians are thinking/feeling right now ♥️
☀️Dear those who don’t live in Florida, but love someone who does. Here are some things to know about hurricanes:
They don't come until they come, so if you ask us how we are 72 hours before we expect the winds to start (or even 12 hours before), don't be surprised if we tell you we're fine.
We're actively preparing, and we're watching the forecast more closely than you are, but we're truly fine at the moment.
Hurricanes are unpredictable. No matter how good the models are, hurricanes often demonstrate a mind of their own. We're always hoping and praying for a turn or "wobble" that sends the monster further from civilization. But if you ask us what's going to happen one or two days from now, we honestly don't know for sure (and neither do the meteorologists).
The entire state can't evacuate. Everyone packing up, jumping into their cars and heading north may seem like a great idea. However, the truth is the roads are jammed, gas is unavailable, hotel rooms sold out, airports close, etc. Plus the most vulnerable folks who live on the coast on the water in the storm's path are in much worse need of evacuation. And imagine evacuating only to find yourself in the car, on the highway, in a massive traffic jam and you run out of gas. No ones coming to save you.
We truly appreciate your love, concern, & offers to stay in your homes, etc. Now the national media is doing a pretty good job of stirring up your anxiety. Our local teams are much calmer and more knowledgeable about how the hurricanes affect our area. They are working nonstop to give us updates and telling us to prepare. We trust them. When the suit comes off, the sleeves are rolled up, and we're told to hunker down, we're ready.
Of course we're worried, but we're trying to do all the right things to prepare and not freak out. Thanks for offering words of love and encouragement (and not jumping on the freak-out wagon - it just makes it harder on us).
Your Florida loved ones ♥️
PS - Ask how we are after it passes! And don’t be surprised if we can’t get back to you ASAP because communication channels can be sketchy post storm.

author: Denis Phillips
text:
Dear everyone who doesn't live in Florida but loves someone who does, here are some things you need to know about hurricanes:
🤔They don't come until they come, so if you ask us how we are 72 hours before we expect the winds to start, don't be surprised if we tell you we're fine. Please believe us. We're actively preparing, and we're watching the forecast more closely than you are, but we're truly fine at the moment.
🌀Hurricanes are unpredictable. No matter how good the models are, hurricanes often demonstrate a mind of their own. We're always hoping and praying for a turn or "wobble" that sends the monster further from civilization. But if you ask us what's going to happen three or four days from now, we honestly don't know for sure (and neither do the meteorologists).
‼️An entire state can't evacuate. Everyone packing up, jumping into their cars and heading north may seem like a great idea. However, the truth is that those of us in "safer" regions generally need to stay put to reserve the roads, gas, hotel rooms, shelters, plane tickets, etc. for the most vulnerable folks who live on the coast in the storm's path (where evacuation orders exist). Some inland folks may choose to leave, but most of us stay put and follow the instructions of our local governments.
🥰We truly appreciate your love and concern, the offers to stay in your homes, etc. Know that the national media is doing a pretty good job of stirring up your anxiety. Our local weather teams are much calmer and more knowledgeable about how the hurricanes affect our area. They are working nonstop to give us updates and telling us to prepare. We trust them. When the tie comes off, the sleeves are rolled up, and we're told to hunker down, we're ready.
🙏Of course we're worried, but we're trying to do all the right things to prepare and not freak out.
✌️Thanks for offering words of love and encouragement (and not jumping on the freak-out wagon - it just makes it harder on us).
💙Your Florida loved ones ❤️
PS. Ask how we are after it passes!

author: Denis Phillips

author: Denis Phillips
text: correct. Nature wants equilibrium. Air rushes into areas of low pressure (storms are low pressure systems. That’s why there is wind… high pressure air rushing into low pressure.) The lower the pressure, the more air that rushes in and the stronger the storm. Think about a fish tank with a divider. One side of the tank is full of water and the other is empty. Remove the divider, and the water rushes in until the level is equal. Air does the same thing. Hurricanes are just incredibly strong storms driven by low pressure. Warm ocean water heats the air at the surface which rises, causing areas of low pressure (the empty side of the fish tank). High pressure air around the storm rushes in… creating hurricane force winds. There is obviously more to it than that, but I hope it helps. This is why hurricanes are stronger when the surface water is warmer. The job of a hurricane is to bleed heat off the ocean. The warmer the ocean, the larger the storm needed to cool it down. Hurricanes are actually an important mechanism by which the Earth cools the ocean. Sadly, we just happen to be in the way

author: Denis Phillips
text: the important thing to remember is don't panic. You don't have to leave the state and it's kind of too late anyway. Get your most important belongings together and find higher ground with a sturdy structure if you are in a low lying area. You still have tomorrow and possibly Wednesday. If you are under a canopy of trees, find the least spot they could fall on as your safe zone. It's almost impossible to leave your county and definatly impossible to leave the state at this point. But you just need a strong structure on high ground as close to your house. Bring your important documents and what ever canned food you have as well as a change of clothing and a few comfort items. Don't try to get on the interstate or highway out of town. They are already backed up and you will be more vulnerable.

author: Denis Phillips
text: The surge (in feet) that meteorologists talk about is based right where the land starts on the water (sea level). In this case, on the Gulf of Mexico next to the water (zero foot mean sea level). Let's say the surge is predicted to be 9 feet above mean sea level. If your house is right on the Gulf, you are in deep doo doo (unless the house is raised above 9 feet). If your house is 10 miles inland AND at 5 feet mean sea level elevation that does not mean with 100% certainty that you will see another 4 foot surge (5 feet + 4 feet = 9 feet) at your house because the surge needs to travel 10 miles inland and there are natural and man made obstacles (trees, buildings, etc..). However, the problem is because the ground is currently very saturated the surge might travel further inland X feet because the ground cannot absorb it. Also, if you live near a pond or river that "adds" to the problem of water surge. I hope I answered your question and did not confuse you.

because of a phenomenon cause, called latent heat release.
Hurricanes often appear to intensify at night due to the increased release of latent heat during the cooler nighttime hours, as the upper atmosphere cools significantly without the sun's radiation, allowing more water vapor to condense into clouds and release significant amounts of heat energy that fuels the storm's intensity; this process is what drives a hurricane's "engine" and can lead to stronger winds and heavier rainfall overnight

text: this is what I always thought too, but Denis explained a couple days ago that it’s not actually accurate. The line is the most likely track and the cone is the margin of error for that track. Meaning that the line (or the eye) could actually be anywhere within the cone. That’s why the cone is bigger further away from the storm (because there’s a bigger margin of error further away from the storm) and smaller closer to the storm. If the cone was just hurricane like conditions, it would be bigger closest to the storm (in a circle).

text:
"We have had the technology to create, control, and steer hurricanes for decades.
“Project Cirrus is the first Official attempt to modify a hurricane. It was run by General Electric with the support of the US military. The official theory was that by changing the temperature outside the eye-wall of a hurricane, which they did by seeding the clouds with various compounds such as silver iodide, a decrease in strong winds will result.
On October 13, 1947, Project Cirrus targeted a hurricane heading out to sea. Approximately 180 pounds of dry ice was dropped into the clouds. The crew then reported a "pronounced modification of the cloud deck". And the hurricane abruptly changed direction and made landfall near Savannah, Georgia. The public blamed the government.
Irving Langmuir, who pioneered General Electric’s atmospheric research department, and admired that the project was about learning how to weaponize the weather, also claimed the reversal of the hurricane had been caused by the project, but the government denied it for twelve years.
After a short delay, the project officially continued. And in 1965, Project Stormfury had targeted Hurricane Betsy for seeding. On that day the storm immediately changed direction and made landfall in Southern Florida. Congress blamed it on Project Stormfury but the government claimed that the hurricane changed direction before they ever had a chance to seed it. And after two months of Congressional hearings, the project was allowed to continue.”

text:
Here's a suggestion to ensure your furry friend's safety during severe tropical storms. Consider purchasing a small pool or inflatable item for under $10 from Walmart or a similar store. Place it in your garage or a secure area of your home. If your garage is noisy and you have a small dog, opt for a toddler pool. You can still use sod or pee pads, but remember to work with your pet and reassure them. Playing soft music during the storm and consulting with your veterinarian can also be helpful. There are various options available, such as special vests, blankets, and medications.
By placing some sod, grass, and perhaps a bit of their waste, you can create a designated area for them to relieve themselves. This will help them sense that it's their space. Place a snack nearby and walk with them to the pool, supporting them as needed. Praise your dog when they use it as their bathroom. This simple measure can provide peace of mind and ensure everyone's safety during inclement weather. Feel free to share this tip with other pet owners, and if you have a different suggestion, please share it as well. We're all in this together. Good luck! The pi k is a soft small sandbox

author: Denis Phillips
text:
From a NOAA page:
Glenda Kuehn I actually just recently put up a post on my page explaining this in detail so I'll copy/paste it below for anyone here who is interested...
While it is true that the majority of hurricanes move more toward the west at this latitude, easterly motions are not unheard of. First, it's important to note WHY most hurricanes spend the majority of their time moving east to west. Most hurricanes, unsurprisingly, spend the majority of their time in the tropics between 0N and 30N latitude. That region of the planet is dominated by a general easterly flow pattern thanks to the easterly trade winds. These winds are a product of the coriolis effect and the low-level section of the Hadley cell, which is the southern most of the 3 major circulation cells that drive large scale motions in Earth's atmosphere. However, if you live in the mid-latitudes where most of the US is located, you'll notice the majority of your weather travels from west to east, in the opposite direction. Unlike the tropics, the mid-latitudes are dominated by the mid-latitude westerlies which are an extension of the Ferrel cell; the second of the 3 major cells.
If you pay attention to most hurricane tracks, they will often move east to west in the tropics thanks to the easterly trade winds and then "recurve" to the north and then east as they gain latitude and move into the mid-latitude westerlies. However, as we get into October and November during the fall, the Hadley cell contracts and the mid-latitude westerlies will start to make it farther south. This means easterly or "backward" motion is more likely
with hurricanes farther to the south.
In Milton's case, a low amplitude shortwave trough embedded in the westerlies will make it into the northern Gulf of Mexico, far enough south to impart an easterly motion on the Hurricane and drag it toward Florida from the west. The front associated with this feature has already been analyzed by the WPC in the northern Gulf. This easterly motion is not unheard of, especially later in the season. There are quite a few examples of tropical cyclones moving more easterly at low latitudes and unsurprisingly, they are almost all in October or November. Hurricane Opal 1997, and Wilma 2005, had a large easterly component of motion in the Gulf of Mexico. Hurricane Michelle 2001 and Paloma 2008 both moved northeast in the Caribbean. But perhaps the most interesting example of an easterly moving hurricane in the tropics is Lenny in 1999, which formed near Jamaica, moved almost due east through the Caribbean, and hit the US and British Virgin Islands from the west as a Cat 4 hurricane.

author: Denis Phillips
text: I have been through one category, four storm ( Hugo)South Carolina, and two category three storms.( Fran & Floyd)North Carolina. Since moving to Florida, I. endured Irma, Ian,iIdalia, Debbie, Helene, and now Milton. There is a great difference in every hurricane, even if they are in the same category. For example, hurricane Fran was more a wind event with a lot of tree and building damage. Hurricane Floyd was the same category as Fran, but it was more a flooding event. Major flooding in rural areas drowned a lot of livestock and farm animals and caused a lot of damage .It all depends on whether you’re getting a direct hit and the intensity of the storm that’s hitting you. If you’re near the water then that’s a whole other ballgame.. depending on how the storm moves in and the storm surge are all factors that could be life-threatening. In the category three hurricanes, it is mostly pine trees that go down first. One can actually hear the trees popping and cracking. In Strong category three and category four hurricanes, very large oak trees can be uprooted. In a category, three shingles, typically around the edges of the roof get ripped off down to the plywood. Trees can be blown down, cutting or slicing through homes. in a strong category, three sheds can be blown apart and blown across properties.. insulation from roof damage blown into trees and telephone poles coming down. Transformers exploding on the poles. Significant power outages. One might have to use pool water flush ones toilet. A category four hurricane you see many ,many trees down damage to homes, windows blown out on older homes. One must consider that hurricanes have a tendency to produce funnel clouds, which may or may not touch the ground and do additional damage. I am not even going to comment on flooding issues. If one lives near a river or a coastline, it is imperative that you know your evacuation zone And paste strict attention to storm surge warnings in your area

text: find out your evacuation zone, and plan accordingly with that info, if you are in zone A , do not wait to find a place to stay, roads get backed up quickly, and gas gets scarce along main roadways. If you aren’t in a major flood zone, fill up your gas tank, have some water, keep your phone and other electronics on the chargers until you loose power. Power banks are a life saver. Pre pack your vehicle with essential and creature comforts that you would want beforehand in case you need to leave in a hurry. If you have pets make sure you have extra food bowls and water for them as well. This one with come and go fast. It’s definitely scary, but if you stay prepared and ready, you will be ok!

author: Denis Phillips
text:
Bring everything inside that could be a projectile.
Fill up your cars with gas and extra gas cans as well for generators etc.
Gather all important documents and place is waterproof protectant and keep with you.
Have cash on hand.
Board up windows if possible.
Get sandbags in place (stack like bricks) and for extra protection stack on top of tarp blocking entry points but make sure you have an escape route if needed.
Have suitcases packed in case of evacuation.
Have medications on hand.
Charge everything you can as far as portable chargers/lanterns/ipad/phones etc.
Know where your hurricane supplies are and get them ready. (Hand crank radio, lanterns, candles, tarps, rope, first aid kit etc)
Unplug all outlets so you don’t fry your electronics from power surges.
Make sure breaker is off when running generator and it’s outside not in your garage and away from your house.
Have food/snacks/bottled water readily available (don’t forget the hand can opener)
Fill sinks and tubs with water for flushing.
Fill old water bottles with water and keep next to sink for hand washing.
Fill Tupperware with water and put in freezer it will help keep your food cold if an outage.
Video and document your property and belongings in case of loss.
Have leashes and crates ready for your pets including records.
Pack food and bowls for them as well. NEVER LEAVE THEM BEHIND.
Safest place is inner most room away from windows.
If you’re in a flood zone and didn’t evacuate stay high and have your kayaks and paddle boards accessible juuuuust in case.
You are allowed to be manic right now.
We’re supposed to take a direct hit to our area as a Cat 3 possibly worse. Who cares if you’re being extra prepared. You’ll thank yourself later.
Hide from wind, run from water. Help each other. We’re all in this together.
I hope this list helped in your preparedness.

author: Denis Phillips
text:
Hi, from a veterinary professional, please add the following for pet owners!
* stock up on needed pet medicine and food. Be aware your local vet clinic will be swamped with similar requests so DO NOT wait til the last minute! ESPECIALLY be sure to fill up on fear-free / anti anxiety meds if your pet needs them!
* make sure your pets' medical records INCLUDING RABIES TAGS are in your "go bag" in case you have to evacuate. If you are assigned to a temporary shelter such as a high school or civic center, many such places *will not let any animal in* if the owner can't provide proof of rabies vaccination on the spot. Your vet clinic will be closed by then so a phone call won't be able to clear anything up. Have DOCUMENTATION on hand!!
* get your cat carrier down out of the attic and clean it NOW. Get your dog's leash and harness ready and check them for fraying and appropriate fit. If you are in an emergency shelter, you will be expected to keep your animals appropriately controlled/ contained. You may be told they cannot be in the shelter with you any more if your animals are making other evacuees feel unsafe. It's not wrong or shameful to own and use a muzzle for your dog if they need it around strangers and scary situations. ❤
* if your pet has never been microchipped, consider having a microchip placed. If they are chipped, reach out to the chip monitoring company to make sure they have your up to date contact information. As a former shelter worker in FL, after every hurricane we would get an influx of lost pets. Many were unchipped or unregistered. We would hold for awhile in case an owner came looking - then up for adoption they would go! If your pet is separated from you in a storm, a microchip is BY FAR the best hope of your getting them back. If you know your pet's chip# but aren't sure if they're registered, here is a tool I use as a vet tech to look it up. It will tell you if the number is registered anywhere, then you can just reach out to the registry company to get your info up to date. (They will charge you a membership fee.)

Denise, I see everyone asking "are we going to get hit in...." directly after you say, it is three days out, I cannot answer any of these questions. So I am going to ask you one you can, "will those in Anchorage Alaska be hit badly by this storm?
After cleaning out mud, sand and water from our little restaurant, crawling behind things, throwing away thousand of dollars in food, if I can still keep my humor, I'm doing OK! But regardless, as our little island will be evacuating tomorrow mid day, I will most definitely prepare MUCH better for Milton. I suggest everyone do the same. Anna Maria Island looks like a war zone. Some, no most, have lost everything they have, many ground level homes could not afford to carry flood insurance. We live just off island, I am so very grateful we have a cool home, ok maybe a few missing food tiles and pool screens, but nothing like these people have lost, not even close. Waste management is doing their best to get the hstreets cleared of all the furniture, appliances, walls counters, cabinets from the streets in time so that if this one hits us, there will be little to no debris to fly around. If you store photos or important papers in your garage or down close to the floor, get them up four or five feet. Holmes Beach police have pallets upon pallets of drinking water, pick some up, it will only go to waste if you don't. Denis, if you are ever out on our little island stop into Minnie's Beach Cafe' in downtown Holmes Beach for the best breakfast on the island on me, for you and your family! You are our man, as I am surely older than you are, you'd best not retire until I am gone to that great Breafast restaurant in the sky!

author: Denis Phillips
text: All - please don’t get Flood Zones (A, AE, X) confused with evacuation zones. Flood zones are established by FEMA and indicate flooding potential for each year. If you are in a Flood Zone A or AE, then you are in what is known as as the 100-year flood zone, which means in any year there is a 1% chance your property will be flooded. If you are in a Flood Zone X, then you are in what is known as the 500-year flood zone, which means that in any year there is a 0.5% chance your property will be flooded. These have nothing to do with hurricanes or other storms. Every property in Florida is in a flood zone. The difference is the probability of flooding each year. The Evacuation Zones of A, B, C, D, etc. are established by County Emergency Management and are primarily based on potential storm surge impacts. This is what you need to pay attention to. The Evacuation Zones are not the same as flood zones. If you live in an Evacuation Zone that is ordered to evacuate, then leave. Go the the website of whatever county you live in and go to their Emergency Management Page to see their evacuation zone map and see where your property is located. Everyone stay safe! As Denis Phillips says- run from the water and hide from the wind. FYI - I am a Certified Floodplain Manager and have previously worked as a Director of Planning in Florida local government assisting with emergency management.

from the Hillsborough county website:
Contents of disaster supply kits vary, depending whether a family has children, pets, or members with disabilities. Generally, everyone's kit should have:
Water for drinking and bathing. Have at least one gallon of water per person, per day, for at least seven days
Food that does not need refrigeration - canned goods, protein bars, peanut butter, etc. - that can feed your family (and pets) for three to seven days
Bring a manual can opener and disposable utensils
A two-week supply of medicines. Keep an updated list of family medicines and dosages, along with doctor and pharmacy phone numbers
Personal hygiene items such as toothbrushes, toothpaste, deodorant, toilet paper, and, if appropriate, diapers and baby wipes
Important papers including driver's license, special medical information, insurance policies, property inventories, and your insurance agent's name and phone number
Consider taking irreplaceable items such as select photographs or keepsakes
At least one complete change of clothing and footwear, and blankets or sleeping bags if staying at a shelter or place without sleeping accommodations
A battery-powered radio and flashlight
A first-aid kit
Cash and coins
When evacuating your home, lock doors and windows; turn off electricity, water, and gas if officials tell you, and tune to local radio and television broadcasts to stay informed.
If you do need to shelter in a County evacuation shelter keep in mind:
Evacuation shelters will not have cots, blankets, or supplies like face masks and hand sanitizer
Each resident may only have space the size of approximately one sleeping bag or 20 square feet
Bring your disaster kit with bedding, medications, hygiene items, and any other specific items you might need for your family.
Alcohol, illegal drugs, and weapons are not permitted
Plan for delays; transportation could take 90 minutes or longer and will have to make multiple stops
Add money to your disaster fund for transportation service. You can always take a shared service like Uber, Lyft, cab companies, etc.
Sheltering in place is a practical option to consider if you live in a sound structure outside of the evacuation area (especially if built since 2002 and not located in a flood prone area)
Evacuate tens of miles instead of hundreds of miles
The Hillsborough County Hurricane Evacuation Assessment Tool (HEAT) which includes real-time open/closed shelter locations, evacuation zones, and HART evacuation routes

author: Denis Phillips
text:
Evacuation routes
Know your evacuation destination and routes. Many states have predetermined evacuation routes and zones.
Emergency kit
Have a readily accessible emergency kit or Go Bag that you can take with you. Backpacks are a good option for storing items, except for food and water.
Pets
Create a plan for your pets and include them in your evacuation plans. If it's not safe for you to stay, it's not safe for your pets either.
Important documents
Have copies of important documents like your insurance policies, house deed, and identification cards.
Battery-powered radio
Have a waterproof, battery-powered, or hand-crank-powered radio with replacement batteries. You can use the radio to stay tuned into local weather advisories.
Evacuation map
Create an evacuation map that shows how to exit the home, where to meet up, and what routes to take out of town.
Other items
Consider bringing cash, checkbook, credit cards, health insurance cards, mobile phones, chargers, laptops, keys, spare glasses or contact lenses

text:
you will. Storm surge only refers to the water surging in from the coast. If you're not on the coast, you're fine.
However, this one is going to have some reallllllly rough winds. It'll be totally different from the last one we just had. If you are in a mobile home, an older house, a house not updated to code in the last 15 years or so, a house in need of repair, or a house surrounded closely by large trees, you will probably want to evacuate.
I've been here in the Bay area my entire life and I'm leaving for this one and I'm not in an evacuation zone. Because I'm in an older house, with shoddy construction, with big dead trees close enough to fall on my bedroom roof. I'm also leaving because Helene didn't flood my little area but it did flood streets all around me to where I couldn't hardly get out of my little area. I've only left one other time in my life but this one is telling me to go because of the house & area I'm in.
I've been through hurricanes in Pinellas Park and had no flooding, didn't lose power and was surrounded by trees but didn't lose any. It really depends on where in Pinellas Park, the age/condition of your house, your property/landscaping and if you have underground power or overhead power lines (mine were underground so no issues ever)

author: Denis Phillips
text:
20 years ago between August 13 and September 25 we had Charley, Frances, Ivan and Jeanne. Charley hit Punta Gorda as a Cat 4. Frances then made landfall near my hometown of Jensen Beach as a large slow Cat 2 and brought much damage from tornadoes then curved around and hit the panhandle. Ivan hit Gulf shores Alabama as a Cat 3 with a storm surge of approximately 15 feet. Took out some of the I 10 bridge. It then also circled back around as a tropical storm over south Florida. Then Jeanne! Smacked into Florida almost the same spot as Frances and followed almost the exact path that Frances took just a few weeks prior!
This is the cycle of the planet we live on. All we can do is learn from it and try our best to work together and help each other through it.

text: One storm at a time.... let's just deal with one storm at a time.....otherwise from what I see here, everyone will just get soooo overwhelmed. People were freaking right after Helene about the blob that formed where she did. Their minds raced to two horrific hurricanes in a row. Didn't happen. author: Denis Phillips
text:
People always think you can predict nature with great accuracy, just because one can predict nature with somewhat accuracy.
They treat it like a sporting event where you get praised if it's exciting or booed if it doesn't live up to expectations. I walked through Coffee Pot Boulevard along the water yesterday after getting back from a trip. The neighborhood had just begun to dump all their furniture and torn pieces of their water logged homes on the street. The water didn't spare you whether you were rich or poor.
The best advice l heard here was to be prepared for anything which you should always do.
I could see on Coffee Pot that all the older low lying homes that weren't protected, along with people with more open first floors, had all their belongings on the street because for whatever reason, without discerning why, they weren't prepared.
I stopped a guy on the street to talk with him and he said that the newer homes that were above seven feet were okay while lower level homes had three feet of water come in. I could see all the drywall cut out four feet high and all the interior destruction that had occurred.
The best advice you can get is to be prepared in advance for everything. Especially depending on where you live geographically.
Not just to be prepared for each individual weather event that comes along that you think might do damage, but to have your home prepared in general so you don't have to worry or exercise extreme energy and preparation for each individual event.
Apathy is a person's great enemy.
Going back to my original point, people are arrogant enough to think that nature can be predicted with extreme accuracy, but nature always wins because it is superior, and it gives what it gives. You just take what it gives. If you're lucky it doesn't give a lot. If you're not so lucky and unprepared it gives a lot, and you get what it gives in the form of damage.
